summary.text: For an arbitrary bound \(B\), apply the hypothesis to \(n=(B+5)!\), obtaining a Sophie Germain prime \(p=6x-1\) and the upper member \(r=6y+1\) of a twin-prime pair with \(p+r=6(B+5)!\). If either \(p\) or \(r\) were at most \(B+2\), it would divide the factorial and hence the other prime, forcing equality and then an impossible size equation; thus \(p>B\) and the lower twin prime \(r-2>B\), so both sets are unbounded and therefore infinite.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
S=\{p\in\mathbb N: p\text{ is prime and }2p+1\text{ is prime}\}
\]
be the set of Sophie Germain primes, and let
\[
T=\{r\in\mathbb N:r\text{ is prime and }r+2\text{ is prime}\}
\]
be the set of lower members of twin-prime pairs.

For a positive integer \(n\), the number \(a(n)\) in the conjecture is the sum, over integers \(x\) with \(1\le x<n\), of the indicator of the following condition. On putting \(y=n-x\), one requires all four numbers
\[
6x-1,\qquad 12x-1,\qquad 6y-1,\qquad 6y+1
\]
to be prime. Since \(x\ge 1\),
\[
12x-1=2(6x-1)+1,
\]
so the first two primality conditions say exactly that \(6x-1\) is a Sophie Germain prime. Since \(x<n\), we have \(y=n-x\ge1\), and
\[
(6y-1)+2=6y+1,
\]
so the last two conditions say that \(6y-1\) is the lower member of a twin-prime pair.

Assume the conjectured positivity statement:
\[
 a(n)>0\qquad\text{for every integer }n>1.
\]
We will prove that both \(S\) and \(T\) are infinite. In fact, we prove the stronger simultaneous unboundedness assertion that, for every \(B\in\mathbb N\), there are \(p\in S\) and \(r\in T\) such that
\[
p>B\quad\text{and}\quad r>B.
\]

We first establish the factorial observation that drives the argument.

**Factorial lemma.** Let \(C,p,q\in\mathbb N\). Suppose that \(p\) and \(q\) are prime and
\[
p+q=6(C+3)!.
\]
Then \(p>C\).

Indeed, suppose for contradiction that \(p\le C\). A prime is positive, and hence, since \(p\le C<C+3\), the number \(p\) occurs among the factors of \((C+3)!\). Thus
\[
p\mid (C+3)!,
\]
and consequently
\[
p\mid 6(C+3)!=p+q.
\]
Because \(p\mid p\), it follows that \(p\mid q\). But \(p\) and \(q\) are both prime, so a prime \(p\) dividing the prime \(q\) must equal \(q\). Therefore \(p=q\). Substitution in the displayed sum gives
\[
2p=6(C+3)!,
\]
and cancellation of \(2\) yields
\[
p=3(C+3)!.
\]
Now \((C+3)!\ge C+3\), so
\[
p=3(C+3)!\ge 3(C+3)>C,
\]
contrary to \(p\le C\). This proves the lemma.

Notice also that the same conclusion applies to the second summand: by interchanging \(p\) and \(q\), if \(p+q=6(C+3)!\) and both summands are prime, then both \(p>C\) and \(q>C\).

We now fix an arbitrary bound \(B\in\mathbb N\). Choose
\[
n=(B+5)!.
\]
This integer is greater than \(1\). By the assumed positivity, \(a(n)>0\). The definition of \(a(n)\) is a finite sum of terms each equal to either \(0\) or \(1\). A positive such sum must have at least one term equal to \(1\). Hence there is an integer \(x\) satisfying
\[
1\le x<n
\]
for which, with
\[
y=n-x,
\]
all four numbers
\[
6x-1,\qquad 12x-1,\qquad 6y-1,\qquad 6y+1
\]
are prime. The inequality \(x<n\) ensures \(y\ge1\), and of course \(x+y=n\).

Set
\[
P=6x-1,\qquad Q=6y+1.
\]
Both \(P\) and \(Q\) are prime, and cancellation of the \(-1\) and \(+1\) gives
\[
P+Q=(6x-1)+(6y+1)=6(x+y)=6n=6(B+5)!.
\]
Write \(C=B+2\). Then \(C+3=B+5\), so this equality has exactly the form
\[
P+Q=6(C+3)!.
\]
The factorial lemma, first as stated and then with the two prime summands interchanged, gives
\[
P>B+2\qquad\text{and}\qquad Q>B+2.
\]

The prime \(P\) is a Sophie Germain prime. Indeed, \(P=6x-1\) is prime by construction, and because \(x\ge1\), ordinary arithmetic in the nonnegative integers gives
\[
2P+1=2(6x-1)+1=12x-1,
\]
which is also prime by construction. Thus \(P\in S\). Moreover,
\[
P>B+2>B,
\]
so this produces a Sophie Germain prime exceeding the arbitrary bound \(B\).

For the twin-prime pair, set
\[
R=6y-1.
\]
The number \(R\) is prime by construction, and
\[
R+2=(6y-1)+2=6y+1=Q
\]
is prime as well. Therefore \(R\in T\). Since \(Q=R+2\) and \(Q>B+2\), we have
\[
R+2>B+2,
\]
and hence \(R>B\). Thus the same decomposition also produces a lower twin prime exceeding \(B\).

We have therefore shown that for every natural-number bound \(B\), there exist simultaneously a Sophie Germain prime \(P\in S\) and a lower twin prime \(R\in T\) with
\[
P>B\quad\text{and}\quad R>B.
\]
It follows that each of \(S\) and \(T\) is unbounded in \(\mathbb N\). Every finite subset of \(\mathbb N\) is bounded—for a nonempty finite set one may take its maximum, while the empty set is trivially bounded. Consequently an unbounded subset of \(\mathbb N\) cannot be finite. Hence \(S\) is infinite and \(T\) is infinite.

Thus, if \(a(n)>0\) for every integer \(n>1\), then there are infinitely many Sophie Germain primes and infinitely many twin-prime pairs.
